body_markdown:
You’ve probably heard the phrase, “all hat, no cattle,” used in some sort of derogatory manner to describe something (or someone) that looks the part but can’t back it up. But if we’re being honest, what’s wrong with a really great hat?


In the car world, myriad vehicles look positively stunning but have less glamorous underpinnings than their bodies might suggest. To a lesser degree, there have been other instances where a plenty capable chassis got a head-turner of a rebody that blew the original design away. We asked our team to sound off on some of their favorite rides that look incredible even if they had more humble origins.


## \[Insert Opera Joke Here\]


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


At the height of its Bubble Economy, Japan’s carmakers were at their most creative. It was the time of the Mazda RX-7 FD, the Honda/Acura NSX… and the Nissan Figaro. Based on the March/Micra platform, the Figaro was actually one of a trio of fabulous retro cars built in Nissan’s Pike factory (along with the S-Cargo and[Be-1](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/nissan-be-1-retro-modern-timeless-original-pike-car/) ). *New York Times* design critic Phil Patton has described them as “the height of postmodernism…unabashedly retro, promiscuously combining elements of the Citroën 2CV, Renault 4, Mini, and Fiat 500.” I love its full-length canvas roof, the shameless aping of Italian design, and really don’t care that it came with a tiny one-liter motor and three-speed auto. — *Nik Berg*


## A Lightweight (and Light-Hearted) Lancia


Broad Arrow


I am not quite as into oddballs and rebodied cars as some of my compatriots, but I do find that one company stands above the rest when we talk about interesting shapes on more pedestrian platforms: Zagato. In fairness, they also put quite a few interesting shapes on some very capable platforms, too. We could easily just make a Zagato list and be done with it ( *turns out,[we did that already](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/celebrating-100-years-of-zagato/) -Ed.)* , but thankfully my colleagues are more creative than I. For my part, I choose the Lancia Fulvia Sport Zagato. Already a visually interesting car with an odd V-4 engine driving the front wheels, and sporting a healthy record in rallying, the regular Fulvia is a compelling car on its own. But then Zagato traded the very recognizable Lancia body for one with a more modern and lean hatchback look, and gave it a very French-looking front end to further confuse casual onlookers. It’s not classically beautiful, but it’s an assertive, sporty design that I can’t help but be drawn to. — *Eddy Eckart*


## Alfa and Touring: A Match Made in Heaven


Broad Arrow


While custom coachwork is on the fringe of my interests, I do have a soft spot for taking something relatively humble and dressing it up with a little extra flair. My favorite example is the 1954 Alfa Romeo 1900C Super Sprint Coupe bodied by Touring. My brain sees a mash-up of a bunch of styling elements best known on other cars, yet somehow it all comes together and doesn’t look like a patchwork job, but rather a sleek, sporty coupe that I would love to be seen driving about town in. Not because it is expensive, but because I think this car has a particularly unique presence that makes even seasoned car spotters tilt their head just a bit. — *Kyle Smith*


## Love for a Luscious Lincoln


Lincoln


I have a huge soft spot for the[Zimmer Quicksilver](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/cars-that-time-forgot-zimmer-quicksilver/) , as I was a caretaker for one many moons ago, but suggesting that the Pontiac Fiero underneath is “humble” is pretty insulting. So I better not.


Another forgotten example is the new Toyota Century SUV, as it’s based on the same TNGA-K platform as the humble[Toyota Camry](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2025-camry-xle-awd-finally-fast-four-fights-for-sedan-supremacy/) . But today’s Camry isn’t necessarily humble, especially with a base price that’s kissing $30 grand.


Instead, I will go with another beloved automobile from my past, the[1984–92 Lincoln Mark VII](https://www.hagerty.com/media/market-trends/hagerty-insider/why-its-time-to-think-about-the-1984-92-lincoln-continental-mark-vii/) . I thought it looked great when I was but a young lad; it was a beast when I was a passenger for a test drive of a 1988 LSC model, and it was an absolute rock star when I finally drove a 1990 LSC for myself. It has so much torque; it was so quiet; the air suspension was isolating but invigorating; everything from the dashboard to the carpet was made out of insanely soft materials, and it had stunningly strong brakes. But at its core, it was just a humble, $3500 1978 Ford Fairmont two-door sedan. — *Sajeev Mehta*


## Meeting of the Meatballs


Flikr | nakhon100


Volvo’s first collaboration with[Bertone](https://www.hagerty.com/media/news/bertone-finally-builds-runabout-six-decades-late/) came in 1975, on the 264 TE limousine, which provided various European heads of state with luxury transport for all their heads-of-state business. Following on from that, the two companies gave us[the 262C](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/klockau-classics/1977-81-volvo-262c-that-most-broughamtastic-volvo/) , from 1977 to ’81—a two-door coupe based on the six-cylinder 260 but with a lowered roof swathed in vinyl, a steeply raked windshield, fat C-pillars, and luxury appointments inside. More than 6600 were built, and they are very much love-it-or-hate-it designs.


Arguably the best-looking Bertone-built Volvo, however, is the 780 coupe, produced from 1986 to 1990 on the 700 platform. Whereas the 262C simply looks like a chopped 240, the 780 has always felt like a more fully baked design—a car that could have only ever been a coupe, despite its sedan and wagon underpinnings. It is elegant and conservative, from a period of design that was leaning more and more “jelly bean.” Like the 262C, the 780 offered a luxurious leather interior with power everything. And like the 262C, it was powered by the disappointing PRV V-6, which perhaps felt more upscale than Volvo’s turbocharged fours at the time, but combined with a four-speed automatic, it was never quite enough to give the 3300-pound coupe the oomph it deserved. Around 8500 were produced, but you seldom see them, which is a shame, because they are fun to look at. — *Stefan Lombard*
